questions.question: The chapter opens with the German proverb 'Wer Ordnung hält, ist nur zu faul zum Suchen.' What does it mean, and how does it frame the chapter?

options.text: 'If you keep things tidily ordered, you're just too lazy to go searching' — it frames the chapter's central trade-off of order versus search, since keeping data sorted is precisely what saves you from scanning
'Order is the first law of nature' — it frames the chapter's argument for normalization
'He who searches, finds' — it frames the chapter's discussion of indexes as search tools
'Tidiness is the enemy of speed' — it frames the argument against sorting

questions.explanation: Order versus search is the axis the whole chapter turns on, from SSTables to B-trees to column sort keys.

questions.question: 'On the most fundamental level, a database needs to do two things.' Which two?

options.text: When you give it some data, it should store the data; when you ask it again later, it should give the data back to you
Enforce a schema and answer queries
Replicate data and tolerate faults
Index data and compress it

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 covered the format in which you give the database your data and the mechanism by which you ask for it again; Chapter 3 takes the database's point of view — how to store what we're given and find it again when asked.

questions.question: Why should an application developer care how the database handles storage internally? State what the chapter concedes and what it nevertheless requires.

options.text: Concedes you're probably not going to implement your own storage engine from scratch; but requires that you select a storage engine appropriate for your application, and to tune one you need a rough idea of what it does under the hood
Requires that you be able to modify the storage engine's source code
Concedes nothing — it argues every developer should write a storage engine once
Requires only that you know the query language

questions.explanation: 'Rough idea' is the hedge, and the chapter's closing paragraphs repeat it — it aims for vocabulary, not expertise in tuning any one engine.

questions.question: Here is the chapter's world's-simplest database. Which single line is responsible for the 'most recent value' semantics? db_set appends 'key,value' to a file; db_get greps for lines starting with the key, strips the prefix with sed, and pipes through tail -n 1.

options.text: The grep, because it matches only the newest line
The tail -n 1, because db_set appends and never overwrites, so old versions of the value survive and the last occurrence is the current one
The sed, because it discards stale prefixes
The append redirection, because it truncates prior values

questions.explanation: Nothing is ever overwritten; recency is recovered at read time by taking the last match. Together the two functions form a key-value store where the value may be a JSON document.

questions.question: The chapter's transcript sets key 123456 once and key 42 twice, then runs cat database. How many lines appear, and why?

options.text: Two lines — one per distinct key
Three lines, because key 42 was written twice and both writes survive: db_set appends rather than overwriting
Four lines, because each write also logs a tombstone
One line, because the file is compacted on read

questions.explanation: The storage format is roughly like a CSV file, ignoring escaping issues.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say db_set has 'pretty good performance for something that is so simple', and what does that make the file?

options.text: Because appending to a file is generally very efficient; the file is a log — an append-only data file, which is what many real databases use internally
Because bash is compiled, and the file is a B-tree
Because grep is optimized, and the file is an index
Because the file is kept in memory, making it a cache

questions.explanation: Real databases have more issues to deal with — concurrency control, reclaiming disk space so the log doesn't grow forever, and handling errors and partially written records — but the basic principle is the same.

questions.question: A boxed note warns about the ambiguity of the word 'log'. What definition does the book adopt?

options.text: The general sense: an append-only sequence of records. It doesn't have to be human-readable, and may be binary and intended only for other programs to read — as opposed to application logs, where text describing what's happening is output
Strictly application logs — human-readable text output describing events
A write-ahead log only
A replication stream between nodes

questions.explanation: Getting this right matters because the book reuses 'log' in this general sense throughout, from storage engines to replication to stream processing.

questions.question: db_get is O(n). A database has 10,000 records and db_get takes 4 ms. On the chapter's model alone, roughly how long at 10 million records?

options.text: 40 ms
400 ms
4 seconds
40 seconds

questions.explanation: 10 million is 1,000 times 10,000, so 4 ms becomes 4,000 ms — 4 seconds. At 10 billion records it is 1,000,000 times, or about 4,000 seconds (roughly an hour and six minutes). The chapter's own gloss on O(n): if you double the number of records n, a lookup takes twice as long. That's not good.

questions.question: Define an index as the chapter does, and state the property that makes adding or dropping one safe.

options.text: Additional metadata on the side which acts as a signpost — an additional structure derived from the primary data. Adding and removing indexes doesn't affect the contents of the database; it only affects the performance of queries
A compressed copy of the primary data, safe to drop because it can be regenerated
A cache of recent query results, safe because it expires
A sorted rewrite of the table, safe because the original is retained

questions.explanation: If you want to search the same data in several different ways, you may need several different indexes on different parts of the data.

questions.question: State 'an important trade-off in storage systems' exactly, and the policy databases adopt because of it.

options.text: Well-chosen indexes speed up read queries, but every index slows down writes — which is why databases don't usually index everything by default, and require the application developer or administrator to choose indexes manually
Indexes speed up writes but slow down reads, so databases index everything by default
Indexes are free on SSDs, so the trade-off only applies to spinning disks
Indexes consume memory but not disk, so the trade-off is about RAM

questions.explanation: It's hard to beat the performance of simply appending to a file, because that's the simplest possible write operation. The goal is the greatest benefit without introducing more overhead than necessary.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with key-value indexes, and what construct does it compare a key-value store to?

options.text: Because although key-value data is not the only kind you can index, it's very common and a useful building block for more complex indexes; key-value stores are quite similar to the dictionary type in most programming languages, usually implemented as a hash map
Because key-value indexes are the only kind used in practice; the comparison is to an array
Because key-value stores are the simplest to implement; the comparison is to a linked list
Because relational indexes are out of scope; the comparison is to a set

questions.explanation: Which prompts the chapter's question: since we already have hash maps for our in-memory data structures, why not use them to index our data on disk?

questions.question: Describe the simplest indexing strategy of Figure 3-1 — the write path and the read path.

options.text: Keep an in-memory hash map where every key maps to a byte offset in the data file. On write, append to the file and update the hash map to reflect the new offset (this works for updating existing keys too). On read, use the hash map to find the offset, seek to that location, and read the value
Keep the whole data file in memory and scan it on every read
Keep a sorted on-disk index and binary search it on every read
Keep a hash map on disk and an offset table in memory

questions.explanation: Figure 3-1 shows storing a log of key-value pairs in a CSV-like format, indexed with an in-memory hash map.

questions.question: 'This is essentially what Bitcask does.' Which product does it belong to, and what must fit in RAM?

options.text: It is the default storage engine in Riak; all the keys must fit in available RAM since the hash map is kept completely in memory, but the values can use more space than there is available memory since they can be loaded from disk with just one disk seek
It is the default engine in Cassandra; both keys and values must fit in RAM
It is Redis's persistence layer; only values must fit in RAM
It is LevelDB's index; neither keys nor values need fit in RAM

questions.explanation: If that part of the data file is already in the filesystem cache, a read doesn't require any disk I/O at all.

questions.question: Which workload does the chapter give as a good fit for Bitcask, and which properties make it fit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The key is the URL of a cat video and the value is the number of times it has been played, incremented on every play
There are a lot of writes, but not too many distinct keys — a large number of writes per key, so it's feasible to keep all keys in memory
The value for each key is updated frequently
Queries are mostly range scans over sorted keys

questions.explanation: Range scans are exactly what a hash index cannot do efficiently — that is one of its two stated limitations.

questions.question: How do we avoid eventually running out of disk space, and what is compaction?

options.text: Break the log into segments by closing a segment file when it reaches a certain size and directing subsequent writes to a new segment file; compaction means throwing away duplicate keys in the log and keeping only the most recent update for each key
Overwrite old entries in place, and compaction means defragmenting the file
Delete the oldest segment periodically; compaction means compressing it
Truncate the log on restart; compaction means rebuilding the hash map

questions.explanation: Figure 3-2 illustrates compaction of a key-value update log counting cat video plays, retaining only the most recent value for each key.

questions.question: Why can compaction run without stopping the database? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Segments are never modified after they have been written, so the merged segment is written to a new file
Merging and compaction can be done in a background thread, and the database can continue to serve read and write requests as normal using the old segment files
After the merge is complete, read requests are switched to the new merged segment and the old segment files can simply be deleted
Compaction acquires a global write lock for only a few milliseconds

questions.explanation: Since compaction often makes segments much smaller, several segments can be merged together at the same time — which is what Figure 3-3 shows.

questions.question: Once there are multiple segments, how is a key found, and what keeps this from degenerating?

options.text: Each segment has its own in-memory hash table; to find a value, check the most recent segment's hash map first, then the second-most-recent, and so on. The merging process keeps the number of segments small, so lookups don't need to check many hash maps
A single global hash map spans all segments, so only one lookup is needed
Segments are searched in parallel, so the count doesn't matter
A Bloom filter replaces the hash maps entirely

questions.explanation: Recency ordering plus bounded segment count is what keeps this efficient.

questions.question: Which implementation issues does the chapter list as important in a real implementation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: File format — a binary format is faster and simpler than CSV, encoding the length of a string in bytes followed by the raw string, without need for escaping
Deleting records — append a special deletion record called a tombstone, so the merging process discards any previous values for that key

Crash recovery — in-memory hash maps are lost on restart; Bitcask speeds up recovery by storing a snapshot of each segment's hash map on disk, since rebuilding by reading every segment end to end might take a long time

Partially written records and concurrency control — Bitcask files include checksums so corrupted parts are detected and ignored, and since writes must be in strictly sequential order there is commonly only one writer thread, while immutable segments can be read concurrently by multiple threads

questions.explanation: Five issues in all — most readers remember only two or three.

questions.question: 'An append-only log seems wasteful at first glance.' Which reasons does the chapter give in its favour? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Appending and segment merging are sequential write operations, generally much faster than random writes, especially on magnetic spinning-disk hard drives — and to some extent sequential writes are also preferable on SSDs
Concurrency and crash recovery are much simpler if segment files are append-only or immutable: you don't have to worry about a crash leaving part of the old and part of the new value spliced together
Merging old segments avoids the problem of data files getting fragmented over time
Append-only logs never need compaction

questions.explanation: Note the hedge in the first reason — 'to some extent' for SSDs. The chapter picks this up again under Comparing B-Trees and LSM-Trees.

questions.question: State both limitations of a hash index. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The hash table must fit in memory, so with a very large number of keys you're out of luck — an on-disk hash map is hard to make perform well because it requires a lot of random access I/O, is expensive to grow when full, and hash collisions require fiddly logic
Range queries are not efficient — you cannot easily scan over all keys between, say, kitty00000 and kitty99999, but have to look up each key individually
Hash indexes cannot support deletions
Hash indexes cannot be compacted

questions.explanation: The next section introduces an indexing structure that has neither limitation.

questions.question: What single requirement turns a log segment into an SSTable, and what is the second requirement?

options.text: Requiring that the sequence of key-value pairs be sorted by key — giving a Sorted String Table, or SSTable. The second requirement, that each key appear only once within each merged segment file, comes free because the compaction process already ensures it
Requiring that segments be compressed; the second is that they be immutable
Requiring that keys be fixed-length; the second is that values be fixed-length
Requiring an in-memory index of every key; the second is checksums

questions.explanation: By default the order is the order the writes came in, and the order of key-value pairs in the file does not matter. At first glance sorting seems to break our ability to use sequential writes — resolved by the memtable.

questions.question: Why does merging SSTables work even when the files exceed available memory?

options.text: The approach is like mergesort: read the input files side by side, look at the first key in each, copy the lowest key to the output file, and repeat. This produces a new merged segment file, also sorted by key
Because the files are memory-mapped, so the OS handles it
Because each file is compressed enough to fit
Because merging only reads the in-memory indexes, not the files

questions.explanation: When the same key appears in several input segments, keep the value from the most recent segment and discard the values in older segments — you can tell which is more recent because each merge takes segments from some period of time, so all the values in one input segment must be more recent than all those in the other.

questions.question: With SSTables you no longer need an index of all the keys in memory. Walk the lookup of 'handiwork' when the sparse index has 'handbag' and 'handsome' but not 'handiwork'.

options.text: You know handiwork must appear between those two keys, so you jump to the offset for handbag and scan from there until you find handiwork — or not, if the key is not present
You binary search the whole file from the start
You must scan the entire segment because the key is missing from the index
You consult a Bloom filter, which returns the exact offset

questions.explanation: One key for every few kilobytes of segment file is sufficient, because a few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly. A footnote notes that if all keys and values were a fixed size you could binary search and avoid the in-memory index entirely — but they are usually variable-length in practice, making it hard to tell where one record ends and the next begins.

questions.question: Why does sorting make block compression natural, and what does each sparse index entry point at?

options.text: Since read requests need to scan over several key-value pairs in the requested range anyway, those records can be grouped into a block and compressed before writing to disk; each entry of the sparse in-memory index then points at the start of a compressed block. Besides saving disk space, compression reduces I/O bandwidth use
Because sorted data is always smaller; each entry points at a row offset
Because compression requires sorted input; each entry points at a checksum
Because blocks must be uniform; each entry points at a segment header

questions.explanation: The shaded area in Figure 3-5 is the block the index entry addresses.

questions.question: 'How do you get your data to be sorted by key in the first place? Our incoming writes can occur in any order.' What is the chapter's answer?

options.text: Maintaining a sorted structure on disk is possible, but maintaining it in memory is much easier — use a well-known in-memory tree data structure such as a red-black tree or AVL tree, which let you insert keys in any order and read them back in sorted order
Sort the file on disk after every write
Require clients to submit writes in sorted order
Use a hash map and sort lazily at read time

questions.explanation: The in-memory tree is the memtable, and it is what reconciles sorted output with sequential writes.

questions.question: State the four-step LSM storage engine. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: On a write, add it to an in-memory balanced tree — the memtable

When the memtable gets bigger than some threshold, typically a few megabytes, write it out to disk as an SSTable file, which becomes the most recent segment; while it is being written out, writes can continue to a new memtable instance
To serve a read, first try the memtable, then the most recent on-disk segment, then the next-older segment, and so on
From time to time, run a merging and compaction process in the background to combine segment files and discard overwritten or deleted values

questions.explanation: Four bullets that together define the whole engine.

questions.question: 'This scheme works very well. It only suffers from one problem.' Name it and the fix.

options.text: If the database crashes, the most recent writes — in the memtable but not yet written out to disk — are lost. The fix is a separate log on disk to which every write is immediately appended; it is not in sorted order, but that doesn't matter because its only purpose is to restore the memtable after a crash. Every time the memtable is written out to an SSTable, the corresponding log can be discarded
Reads become slow; the fix is Bloom filters
Disk fills up; the fix is compaction
Keys are unsorted; the fix is a red-black tree

questions.explanation: Sortedness is unnecessary in the recovery log precisely because it is never queried, only replayed.

questions.question: Which facts does the chapter give about the lineage of LSM-trees? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The algorithm is essentially what is used in LevelDB and RocksDB, key-value storage engine libraries designed to be embedded into other applications; LevelDB can be used in Riak as an alternative to Bitcask
Similar storage engines are used in Cassandra and HBase, both of which were inspired by Google's Bigtable paper, which introduced the terms SSTable and memtable
The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) was named by Patrick O'Neil et al., building on earlier work on log-structured filesystems
The LSM-tree was first described in Codd's 1970 relational paper

questions.explanation: Storage engines based on the principle of merging and compacting sorted files are often called LSM storage engines.

questions.question: How does Lucene reuse the SSTable idea?

options.text: Lucene, the indexing engine for full-text search used by Elasticsearch and Solr, stores its term dictionary this way: the key is a word (a term) and the value is the list of IDs of all documents containing the word (the postings list), kept in SSTable-like sorted files that are merged in the background as needed
Lucene stores documents as SSTables and terms as B-trees
Lucene uses SSTables only for caching query results
Lucene uses hash indexes, not SSTables

questions.explanation: The full-text index mechanism is much more complex than a key-value index, but based on a similar idea of sorted, merged files.

questions.question: Which access pattern is slow on an LSM-tree, and what fixes it?

options.text: Looking up keys that do not exist: you have to check the memtable, then all segments all the way back to the oldest, possibly reading from disk for each one, before you can be sure the key doesn't exist. Storage engines often use Bloom filters — a memory-efficient data structure for approximating the contents of a set, which can tell you if a key does not appear, saving many unnecessary disk reads for nonexistent keys
Range scans; fixed by sparse indexes
Sequential writes; fixed by the write-ahead log
Point lookups of existing keys; fixed by compaction

questions.explanation: A Bloom filter can return false positives but never false negatives, which is exactly the right asymmetry here.

questions.question: Match the two compaction strategies to their systems and describe how each works.

options.text: Size-tiered: newer and smaller SSTables are successively merged into older and larger SSTables — used by HBase. Leveled: the key range is split up into smaller SSTables and older data is moved into separate levels, so compaction proceeds more incrementally and uses less disk space — used by LevelDB (hence its name) and RocksDB. Cassandra supports both
Size-tiered is used by LevelDB; leveled by HBase; Cassandra supports neither
Both strategies are used only by Cassandra
Leveled merges smaller into larger; size-tiered splits by key range

questions.explanation: There are many subtleties, but the basic idea is simple and effective.

questions.question: Summarize the chapter's closing claims for LSM-trees.

options.text: The basic idea — keeping a cascade of SSTables that are merged in the background — is simple and effective. It works well even when the dataset is much bigger than the available memory, and since data is stored in sorted order it can efficiently perform range queries; and because the disk writes are sequential it can support remarkably high write throughput
LSM-trees are faster for reads and slower for writes than B-trees
LSM-trees require the dataset to fit in memory
LSM-trees cannot support range queries

questions.explanation: Two capabilities highlighted: range queries from sortedness, and write throughput from sequentiality.

questions.question: How does the chapter position log-structured indexes against B-trees, and what dates does it cite?

options.text: Log-structured indexes are gaining acceptance but are not the most common type of index; the most widely used indexing structure is the B-tree, introduced in 1970 and called 'ubiquitous' less than 10 years later. B-trees have stood the test of time very well and remain the standard index implementation in almost all relational databases, with many nonrelational databases using them too
Log-structured indexes are now the most common; B-trees date from 1980
B-trees were introduced in 1979 and called ubiquitous in 1970
Both are equally common; B-trees date from 1990

questions.explanation: The 'ubiquitous' reference is Douglas Comer's 1979 survey.

questions.question: What do B-trees and SSTables share, and where do they diverge — with the unit sizes for each?

options.text: Both keep key-value pairs sorted by key, allowing efficient key-value lookups and range queries. But that's where the similarity ends: log-structured indexes break the database into variable-size segments, typically several megabytes or more, written sequentially; B-trees break it into fixed-size blocks or pages, traditionally 4 KB (sometimes bigger), read or written one page at a time — corresponding more closely to the underlying hardware, as disks are also arranged in fixed-size blocks
Both use fixed-size 4 KB pages; they diverge only in sort order
Both use variable-size segments; they diverge in compression
Neither keeps keys sorted; they diverge in durability

questions.explanation: Fixed-size pages versus variable-size segments is the root of every other difference between the two families.

questions.question: Define branching factor, give its value in Figure 3-6, and its typical value in practice.

options.text: The number of references to child pages in one page of the B-tree; it is six in Figure 3-6; in practice it depends on the amount of space required to store the page references and the range boundaries, and is typically several hundred
The number of levels in the tree; two in Figure 3-6; typically four
The number of keys per leaf page; six in Figure 3-6; typically thousands
The ratio of interior to leaf pages; six in Figure 3-6; typically ten

questions.explanation: A page address is the location that allows one page to refer to another — similar to a pointer, but on disk instead of in memory.

questions.question: Describe the B-tree update path and insert path.

options.text: To update an existing key, search for the leaf page containing that key, change the value in that page, and write the page back to disk — any references to that page remain valid. To add a new key, find the page whose range encompasses it and add it there; if there isn't enough free space, the page is split into two half-full pages and the parent page is updated to reflect the new subdivision of key ranges
Both append to a log and update the index later
Updates split pages; inserts overwrite in place
Both require rewriting the root page

questions.explanation: Figure 3-7 shows growing a B-tree by splitting a page. A footnote notes that inserting a key is reasonably intuitive, but deleting one while keeping the tree balanced is somewhat more involved.

questions.question: A four-level tree of 4 KB pages with a branching factor of 500 can store up to how much, and what is the typical depth?

options.text: 256 TB — 500 to the fourth power is 62,500,000,000 pages, times 4 KB is about 2.56 times 10 to the 14th bytes. The algorithm keeps the tree balanced, so a B-tree with n keys always has a depth of O(log n), and most databases fit into a B-tree three or four levels deep
256 GB, with a typical depth of six or seven levels
2.56 PB, with a typical depth of two levels
25.6 TB, with a typical depth of ten levels

questions.explanation: So you don't need to follow many page references to find the page you're looking for.

questions.question: State the B-tree's fundamental write operation and the assumption it rests on.

options.text: Overwrite a page on disk with new data, assuming the overwrite does not change the location of the page, so all references to that page remain intact. This is in stark contrast to log-structured indexes such as LSM-trees, which only append to files and never modify files in place
Append the new page and update the parent pointer
Write the page to a new location and garbage-collect the old one
Buffer the write in memory and flush on commit

questions.explanation: On a magnetic hard drive this means moving the disk head, waiting for the right position on the spinning platter, and overwriting the appropriate sector. On SSDs it is somewhat more complicated, since an SSD must erase and rewrite fairly large blocks of a storage chip at a time.

questions.question: Why can a single logical insert require several page overwrites, and what structure fixes the resulting danger?

options.text: If a page is split because an insertion made it overfull, you need to write the two pages that were split and also overwrite their parent page. If the database crashes after only some of the pages have been written you end up with a corrupted index — for example an orphan page that is not a child of any parent. The fix is a write-ahead log (WAL, also known as a redo log): an append-only file to which every B-tree modification must be written before it can be applied to the pages of the tree itself, used after a crash to restore the B-tree to a consistent state
Because pages are compressed; the fix is checksums
Because the root must be rewritten; the fix is copy-on-write
Because leaves are linked; the fix is sibling pointers

questions.explanation: Crucially, the WAL is written before the pages, not after.

questions.question: What concurrency problem does update-in-place create, and why are log-structured approaches simpler here?

options.text: Careful concurrency control is required if multiple threads access the B-tree at the same time, otherwise a thread may see the tree in an inconsistent state — typically handled by protecting the tree's data structures with latches (lightweight locks). Log-structured approaches are simpler because they do all the merging in the background without interfering with incoming queries and atomically swap old segments for new segments
B-trees require distributed consensus; log-structured engines do not
B-trees need serializable transactions; log-structured engines are single-threaded
Log-structured engines need latches too, making them equally complex

questions.explanation: Immutability is what removes the need for reader-writer coordination.

questions.question: Which B-tree optimizations does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Copy-on-write — instead of overwriting pages and maintaining a WAL for crash recovery, a modified page is written to a different location and a new version of the parent pages is created pointing at the new location (LMDB does this)

Abbreviated keys — interior pages need only enough information to act as boundaries between key ranges, so keys can be abbreviated rather than stored in full, packing more keys into a page for a higher branching factor and thus fewer levels

Sequential leaf layout and sibling pointers — trying to lay out leaf pages in sequential order on disk so large scans avoid a seek per page (hard to maintain as the tree grows), and giving leaf pages references to their left and right siblings so keys can be scanned in order without jumping back to parent pages
Fractal trees — variants that borrow some log-structured ideas to reduce disk seeks, and which have nothing to do with fractals

questions.explanation: Five optimizations, 'to mention just a few'. By contrast, LSM-trees rewrite large segments of storage in one go, making it easier for them to keep sequential keys close to each other on disk.

questions.question: Explain the causal chain from abbreviating interior-page keys to fewer disk reads.

options.text: Shorter keys mean more keys fit in one fixed-size page, which means more references to child pages, which means a higher branching factor and thus fewer levels — and since B-trees read or write one page at a time, fewer levels means fewer page references to follow, hence fewer disk reads
Shorter keys compress better, so pages load faster
Shorter keys reduce latch contention
Shorter keys allow sibling pointers to be inlined

questions.explanation: The whole chain rests on the fixed page size: space saved on keys converts directly into branching factor.

questions.question: True or false, per the chapter: a B-tree page's location changes when it is overwritten; the WAL must be written after the tree pages are updated; fractal trees are named for their self-similar geometry.

options.text: All three are false — the overwrite is assumed not to change the page's location, the WAL must be written before the pages, and fractal trees have nothing to do with fractals
All three are true
Only the first is false
Only the third is false

questions.explanation: The chapter does state as true that 4 KB is the traditional page size and pages may be bigger.

questions.question: State the rule of thumb comparing LSM-trees and B-trees, and note the hedge.

options.text: As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, whereas B-trees are thought to be faster for reads — the hedged verb 'thought to be' matters, because reads are typically slower on LSM-trees as they have to check several different data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction. Benchmarks are often inconclusive and sensitive to details of the workload, so you need to test systems with your particular workload
LSM-trees are faster for both reads and writes, with no hedge
B-trees are definitively faster for reads, as benchmarks consistently show
The two are indistinguishable in practice

questions.explanation: The chapter also notes B-tree implementations are generally more mature than LSM-tree implementations, which confounds the comparison.

questions.question: Define write amplification, and state how many times a B-tree writes each piece of data at minimum.

options.text: One write to the database resulting in multiple writes to the disk over the course of the database's lifetime. A B-tree index must write every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page itself, and perhaps again as pages are split
The ratio of index size to data size; a B-tree writes data once
The growth of the log over time; a B-tree writes data three times minimum
The number of pages touched per query; a B-tree writes data four times

questions.explanation: There's also overhead from writing an entire page at a time even if only a few bytes changed, and some storage engines even overwrite the same page twice to avoid a partially updated page in the event of a power failure. Log-structured indexes also rewrite data multiple times due to repeated compaction and merging of SSTables.

questions.question: Which two distinct costs of write amplification does the chapter name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hardware wear — of particular concern on SSDs, which can only overwrite blocks a limited number of times before wearing out

Throughput — in write-heavy applications the bottleneck might be the rate at which the database can write to disk, so the more a storage engine writes, the fewer writes per second it can handle within the available disk bandwidth
Increased read latency from fragmentation
Higher memory consumption for the write buffer

questions.explanation: One cost is to the device, the other to the workload.

questions.question: Give both reasons LSM-trees sustain higher write throughput, including the hedge on the first.

options.text: First, they sometimes have lower write amplification — although this depends on the storage engine configuration and workload. Second, they sequentially write compact SSTable files rather than having to overwrite several pages in the tree. This difference is particularly important on magnetic hard drives, where sequential writes are much faster than random writes
They always have lower write amplification and never need a WAL
They keep all data in memory and write asynchronously
They compress better and skip the merge step

questions.explanation: The explicit hedge on write amplification is the chapter being careful not to overclaim.

questions.question: Why do LSM-trees produce smaller files, where does a B-tree lose space, and what does SSD firmware do that partly neutralizes the argument?

options.text: LSM-trees can be compressed better and thus often produce smaller files than B-trees. B-tree storage engines leave some disk space unused due to fragmentation: when a page is split, or when a row cannot fit into an existing page, some space in a page remains unused. Since LSM-trees are not page-oriented and periodically rewrite SSTables to remove fragmentation, they have lower storage overheads, especially with leveled compaction. On many SSDs the firmware internally uses a log-structured algorithm to turn random writes into sequential writes, so the storage engine's write pattern has less pronounced impact — but lower write amplification and reduced fragmentation are still advantageous, since representing data more compactly allows more read and write requests within the available I/O bandwidth
B-trees compress better; LSM-trees lose space to segment overlap; SSD firmware makes the difference vanish entirely
Neither compresses; the difference is purely in seek behaviour
LSM-trees waste space on tombstones, which SSD firmware reclaims

questions.explanation: The firmware absorbs part of the write-pattern advantage but not the compactness advantage.

questions.question: State the first downside of log-structured storage, and where the damage shows up.

options.text: The compaction process can sometimes interfere with the performance of ongoing reads and writes. Although storage engines try to perform compaction incrementally and without affecting concurrent access, disks have limited resources, so a request may need to wait while the disk finishes an expensive compaction operation. The impact on throughput and average response time is usually small, but at higher percentiles response times can be quite high — and B-trees can be more predictable
Compaction corrupts data, requiring checksums
Compaction requires taking the database offline
Compaction increases average response time dramatically while leaving percentiles unaffected

questions.explanation: The chapter cross-references Describing Performance on page 13 — the tail-latency argument from Chapter 1 applied to storage.

questions.question: Describe the failure mode when compaction can't keep up at high write throughput.

options.text: A disk's finite write bandwidth is shared between the initial write (logging and flushing a memtable) and the compaction threads running in the background. On an empty database the full bandwidth can be used for the initial write, but the bigger the database gets the more bandwidth compaction requires. If compaction is not configured carefully it can fail to keep up with incoming writes: the number of unmerged segments on disk keeps growing until you run out of disk space, and reads also slow down because they need to check more segment files. Typically SSTable-based engines do not throttle the rate of incoming writes even when compaction cannot keep up, so you need explicit monitoring to detect this
The database automatically throttles writes, so nothing breaks
Compaction gets priority, so writes fail with errors
Reads speed up because fewer merges occur

questions.explanation: The absence of back-pressure is what makes this an operational duty rather than a self-correcting condition.

questions.question: Give the B-tree advantage that has nothing to do with speed.

options.text: Each key exists in exactly one place in the index, whereas a log-structured storage engine may have multiple copies of the same key in different segments. This makes B-trees attractive in databases that want to offer strong transactional semantics: in many relational databases transaction isolation is implemented using locks on ranges of keys, and in a B-tree index those locks can be directly attached to the tree
B-trees never need a write-ahead log
B-trees can be compressed more aggressively
B-trees support range queries, unlike LSM-trees

questions.explanation: Uniqueness of location is what makes a lock on a key range well-defined. Chapter 7 discusses this in more detail.

questions.question: Summarize the section's closing judgment on B-trees versus LSM-trees.

options.text: B-trees remain very ingrained in the architecture of databases and provide consistently good performance for many workloads, so it's unlikely they will go away anytime soon; in new datastores, log-structured indexes are becoming increasingly popular. There is no quick and easy rule for determining which type of storage engine is better for your use case, so it is worth testing empirically
LSM-trees are the clear winner and B-trees are legacy
B-trees win for all workloads
The chapter gives a decision table that settles the question

questions.explanation: The chapter predicts, concedes, and then explicitly refuses to give a rule.

questions.question: Key-value indexes are analogous to what, and what does a primary key uniquely identify in each of the three data models?

options.text: A primary key index in the relational model, which uniquely identifies one row in a relational table, one document in a document database, or one vertex in a graph database. Other records can refer to that row, document or vertex by its primary key (or ID), and the index is used to resolve such references
A secondary index; it identifies a column in each model
A clustered index; it identifies a page in each model
A covering index; it identifies a partition in each model

questions.explanation: Primary key indexes are the base case; secondary indexes are the variation the next section covers.

questions.question: How are secondary indexes created in relational databases, and why are they crucial?

options.text: With the CREATE INDEX command, and they are often crucial for performing joins efficiently — for example the user_id columns in the Figure 2-1 example from Chapter 2, used to find all the rows belonging to the same user in each of the tables
Automatically by the optimizer; they are crucial for durability
With ALTER TABLE; they are crucial for enforcing uniqueness
They cannot be created after table creation

questions.explanation: Joins are the workload that makes secondary indexes non-optional in relational schemas.

questions.question: A secondary index can easily be constructed from a key-value index. What is the main difference, and what are the two ways to solve it?

options.text: In a secondary index the keys are not unique — there might be many rows with the same key. That can be solved either by making each value in the index a list of matching row identifiers (like a postings list in a full-text index), or by making each key unique by appending a row identifier to it. Either way, both B-trees and log-structured indexes can be used as secondary indexes
Secondary indexes cannot be sorted; solved by hashing or by partitioning
Secondary indexes cannot be updated; solved by rebuilding or by versioning
Secondary indexes must be clustered; solved by covering or by interleaving

questions.explanation: Non-uniqueness is the only structural difference, and the index type is orthogonal to it.

questions.question: Define a heap file and describe what happens when an updated value grows too large to overwrite in place.

options.text: The value in an index can be either the actual row or a reference to the row stored elsewhere; in the latter case the place where rows are stored is known as a heap file, which stores data in no particular order (it may be append-only, or may keep track of deleted rows to overwrite them later). The heap file approach avoids duplicating data when multiple secondary indexes are present. A record can be overwritten in place provided the new value is not larger than the old; if it is larger, it probably needs to be moved to a new location in the heap, and then either all indexes need updating to point at the new heap location, or a forwarding pointer is left behind in the old location
A heap file is a sorted file; oversized values are compressed
A heap file is an in-memory structure; oversized values are spilled to disk
A heap file is the write-ahead log; oversized values are split across pages

questions.explanation: The forwarding pointer is the cheaper option, at the cost of an extra hop on read.

questions.question: Define a clustered index and give the chapter's two concrete product behaviours.

options.text: A clustered index stores the indexed row directly within an index, used when the extra hop from index to heap file is too much of a performance penalty for reads. In MySQL's InnoDB the primary key of a table is always a clustered index, and secondary indexes refer to the primary key rather than a heap file location. In SQL Server you can specify one clustered index per table
A clustered index groups rows by partition key; InnoDB and SQL Server both allow many per table
A clustered index is a covering index; InnoDB forbids them
A clustered index sorts the heap file; SQL Server maintains one automatically per column

questions.explanation: 'Clustered' means the row lives inside the index, eliminating the indirection.

questions.question: What sits between a clustered and a nonclustered index, and what is the phrase for when it succeeds?

options.text: A covering index or index with included columns, which stores some of a table's columns within the index. This allows some queries to be answered by using the index alone — in which case the index is said to cover the query
A partial index; it is said to satisfy the query
A concatenated index; it is said to span the query
A sparse index; it is said to short-circuit the query

questions.explanation: A clustered index stores all row data within the index; a nonclustered index stores only references.

questions.question: Clustered and covering indexes speed up reads. Which costs does the chapter attach? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They require additional storage
They can add overhead on writes
Databases need additional effort to enforce transactional guarantees, because applications should not see inconsistencies due to the duplication
They prevent the use of range queries

questions.explanation: Any kind of duplication of data carries these three costs.

questions.question: Define a concatenated index, give the chapter's analogy, and state which query shapes work.

options.text: It simply combines several fields into one key by appending one column to another, with the index definition specifying in which order the fields are concatenated. The analogy is an old-fashioned paper phone book providing an index from (lastname, firstname) to phone number: you can use it to find all the people with a particular last name, or all the people with a particular lastname-firstname combination, but it is useless if you want to find all the people with a particular first name
It indexes each column separately; all three query shapes work equally
It hashes the columns together; only exact full-key matches work
It sorts by the last column first; first-name queries work but last-name queries do not

questions.explanation: Order is everything: prefix queries work, suffix queries don't. A one-column index is not sufficient when you need to query multiple columns simultaneously.

questions.question: A restaurant search filters latitude within a narrow band AND longitude within a narrow band. Why can't a standard B-tree or LSM-tree answer it efficiently?

options.text: Because there are two range predicates that must be satisfied at once. A standard index can give you either all the restaurants in a range of latitudes (but at any longitude), or all the restaurants in a range of longitudes (but anywhere between the North and South poles), but not both simultaneously
Because floating-point values cannot be indexed
Because the predicates use AND rather than OR
Because latitude and longitude are stored in separate tables

questions.explanation: This is exactly where a concatenated index falls short, and where multi-dimensional indexes earn their place.

questions.question: How are multi-dimensional indexes actually built, and what stack does PostGIS use?

options.text: One option is to translate a two-dimensional location into a single number using a space-filling curve and then use a regular B-tree index; more commonly, specialized spatial indexes such as R-trees are used. PostGIS implements geospatial indexes as R-trees using PostgreSQL's Generalized Search Tree indexing facility
Only space-filling curves are used; PostGIS uses a B-tree on a Hilbert curve
Only quadtrees are used; PostGIS uses a quadtree extension
Multi-dimensional indexes are not implemented in practice

questions.explanation: The chapter says it doesn't have space to describe R-trees in detail, but there is plenty of literature on them.

questions.question: Which non-geographic multi-dimensional index examples does the chapter give, and what would a one-dimensional index force you to do for the weather query? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Ecommerce — a three-dimensional index on the dimensions (red, green, blue) to search for products in a certain range of colors
Weather — a two-dimensional index on (date, temperature) to find all observations during 2013 where the temperature was between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius

With a one-dimensional index you would have to either scan over all the records from 2013 regardless of temperature and then filter them by temperature, or vice versa; a 2D index could narrow down by timestamp and temperature simultaneously. This technique is used by HyperDex
Genomics — a four-dimensional index on nucleotide positions

questions.explanation: An interesting idea is that multi-dimensional indexes are not just for geographic locations.

questions.question: What shared assumption do all the indexes so far make, and what specific capabilities do full-text search engines add?

options.text: They all assume you have exact data and allow you to query for exact values of a key, or a range of values with a sort order — they don't let you search for similar keys such as misspelled words, which requires different fuzzy querying techniques. Search engines allow a query for one word to be expanded to include synonyms, ignore grammatical variations, search for occurrences of words near each other in the same document, and support other features that depend on linguistic analysis of the text. Lucene is able to search text for words within a certain edit distance, where an edit distance of 1 means that one letter has been added, removed, or replaced
They assume sorted data, and search engines add compression
They assume unique keys, and search engines add duplicates
They assume numeric keys, and search engines add strings

questions.explanation: Exactness is the shared assumption; fuzziness needs a different data structure.

questions.question: How does Lucene's in-memory index differ from LevelDB's, and what transformation does Lucene apply?

options.text: Both keep a small in-memory index telling queries at which offset in the sorted file to look for a key. In LevelDB this index is a sparse collection of some of the keys; in Lucene it is a finite state automaton over the characters in the keys, similar to a trie. That automaton can be transformed into a Levenshtein automaton, which supports efficient search for words within a given edit distance
Lucene uses a sparse key collection; LevelDB uses a trie
Lucene has no in-memory index; LevelDB has a full key index
Both use Bloom filters, differing only in size

questions.explanation: Other fuzzy search techniques go in the direction of document classification and machine learning; the chapter refers you to an information retrieval textbook.

questions.question: State the chapter's complaint about disks and the two advantages that make us tolerate them — and which one is eroding.

options.text: Disks are awkward to deal with — both magnetic disks and SSDs need their data laid out carefully if you want good read and write performance. We tolerate them because they are durable (contents are not lost if the power is turned off) and have a lower cost per gigabyte than RAM. As RAM becomes cheaper, the cost-per-gigabyte argument is eroded: many datasets are simply not that big, so it's feasible to keep them entirely in memory, potentially distributed across several machines — leading to in-memory databases
Disks are slow; the advantages are capacity and reliability, and reliability is eroding
Disks are expensive; the advantages are speed and durability, and speed is eroding
Disks are fragile; the advantages are cost and portability, and portability is eroding

questions.explanation: It is cost per gigabyte, not durability, that RAM's falling price undermines.

questions.question: Contrast Memcached with in-memory databases that aim for durability, listing the durability mechanisms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Memcached is intended for caching use only, where it's acceptable for data to be lost if a machine is restarted
Durability can be achieved with special hardware such as battery-powered RAM, or by writing a log of changes to disk
Durability can be achieved by writing periodic snapshots to disk, or by replicating the in-memory state to other machines
Durability is impossible for in-memory databases by definition

questions.explanation: When an in-memory database is restarted it needs to reload its state, either from disk or over the network from a replica — unless special hardware is used.

questions.question: An in-memory database may write to disk. Why is it still called in-memory?

options.text: Because the disk is merely used as an append-only log for durability, and reads are served entirely from memory. The disk file also has the operational advantage that it can easily be backed up, inspected, and analyzed by external utilities
Because the writes are asynchronous
Because the disk holds only the index, not the data
Because the disk file is memory-mapped

questions.explanation: The read path, not the write path, is what defines the category.

questions.question: Match the in-memory products to what the chapter says about them.

options.text: VoltDB, MemSQL and Oracle TimesTen are in-memory databases with a relational model, whose vendors claim big performance improvements by removing all the overheads associated with managing on-disk data structures; RAMCloud is an open source in-memory key-value store with durability, using a log-structured approach for the data in memory as well as the data on disk; Redis and Couchbase provide weak durability by writing to disk asynchronously
Redis and Couchbase are relational; VoltDB and MemSQL are key-value stores with strong durability
RAMCloud is relational; TimesTen is a cache with no durability
All six offer strong durability through battery-backed RAM

questions.explanation: Note the wording on the relational group: the chapter reports the vendors' claim rather than endorsing it.

questions.question: Why are in-memory databases fast? Give the reason most people assume and the real one.

options.text: Counterintuitively, the performance advantage is not because they don't need to read from disk — even a disk-based storage engine may never need to read from disk if you have enough memory, because the operating system caches recently used disk blocks in memory anyway. Rather, they can be faster because they avoid the overheads of encoding in-memory data structures in a form that can be written to disk
Because RAM has lower latency than disk, which is the whole story
Because they skip the write-ahead log
Because they use vectorized processing

questions.explanation: Serialization overhead, not I/O, is the real cost being avoided.

questions.question: Besides performance, what does the chapter call 'another interesting area' for in-memory databases?

options.text: Providing data models that are difficult to implement with disk-based indexes — for example Redis offers a database-like interface to various data structures such as priority queues and sets, and because it keeps all data in memory its implementation is comparatively simple
Providing stronger transactional guarantees than disk-based systems
Providing built-in replication
Providing schema-on-read flexibility

questions.explanation: Keeping everything in memory makes exotic data structures cheap to implement.

questions.question: Describe the anti-caching approach and the limitation it still has.

options.text: It evicts the least recently used data from memory to disk when there is not enough memory, and loads it back into memory when accessed again — similar to what operating systems do with virtual memory and swap files, but the database can manage memory more efficiently than the OS because it works at the granularity of individual records rather than entire memory pages. It still requires indexes to fit entirely in memory, like the Bitcask example at the beginning of the chapter
It compresses cold data in place; it still requires the whole dataset to fit in memory
It replicates cold data to other machines; it still requires uniform access patterns
It is identical to OS swapping with no advantages; it requires no indexes

questions.explanation: Record-level granularity is the improvement over OS paging; the in-memory index requirement is the residual constraint.

questions.question: What technology does the chapter say may force further storage engine redesign, and how confidently?

options.text: Non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies — further changes will probably be needed if they become more widely adopted; at present this is a new area of research, but worth keeping an eye on in the future
Quantum storage, which it says will certainly force a redesign
Shingled magnetic recording, which it says has already forced a redesign
Persistent GPU memory, which it dismisses

questions.explanation: Deliberately hedged — 'probably', 'new area of research'.

questions.question: Where does the word 'transaction' come from, and what is the modern definition?

options.text: From the early days of business data processing, where a write typically corresponded to a commercial transaction taking place: making a sale, placing an order with a supplier, paying an employee's salary. As databases expanded into areas that didn't involve money changing hands the term nevertheless stuck, and now refers to a group of reads and writes that form a logical unit
From accounting double-entry bookkeeping; it now means an atomic write
From telecommunications switching; it now means a request-response pair
From ACID theory; it now means an isolated operation

questions.explanation: A useful reminder that the word carries no technical guarantee by itself.

questions.question: A boxed note makes a careful disclaimer about ACID. What does it deny and what does it assert?

options.text: It denies that a transaction needs to have ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) properties; transaction processing just means allowing clients to make low-latency reads and writes — as opposed to batch processing jobs, which only run periodically, for example once per day
It asserts that all transactions are ACID by definition
It denies that batch processing exists
It asserts that ACID is required for OLTP but not OLAP

questions.explanation: Forward references: ACID properties in Chapter 7, batch processing in Chapter 10.

questions.question: Describe the OLTP access pattern and expand the acronym.

options.text: An application typically looks up a small number of records by some key, using an index; records are inserted or updated based on the user's input. Because these applications are interactive, the access pattern became known as online transaction processing (OLTP)
An application scans many records and aggregates them; the acronym is online table processing
An application writes in bulk once per day; the acronym is offline transaction processing
An application reads whole tables into memory; the acronym is optimized lookup transaction processing

questions.explanation: Even as databases came to hold comments on blog posts, actions in a game, contacts in an address book and so on, the basic access pattern remained similar to processing business transactions.

questions.question: Describe the analytic access pattern and its example queries. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A query needs to scan over a huge number of records, only reading a few columns per record, and calculates aggregate statistics such as count, sum or average rather than returning the raw data to the user
What was the total revenue of each of our stores in January? How many more bananas than usual did we sell during our latest promotion?
Which brand of baby food is most often purchased together with brand X diapers?
What is the current balance of account 12345?

questions.explanation: The last one is an OLTP query. Analytic queries are often written by business analysts and feed into reports that help management make better decisions — business intelligence.

questions.question: Expand OLAP and state the hedge the chapter makes about the OLTP/OLAP distinction.

options.text: Online analytic processing; the difference between OLTP and OLAP is not always clear-cut, but some typical characteristics are listed in Table 3-1
Offline analytic processing; the distinction is absolute
Optimized aggregate processing; the distinction is only about data volume
Online aggregate protocol; the distinction is vendor-specific

questions.explanation: A footnote notes the meaning of 'online' in OLAP is unclear; it probably refers to the fact that queries aren't just for predefined reports — analysts use the OLAP system interactively for explorative queries. Note the double hedge: 'unclear' and 'probably'.

questions.question: In Table 3-1, which dataset sizes does the chapter give for OLTP and OLAP?

options.text: Gigabytes to terabytes for OLTP; terabytes to petabytes for OLAP
Megabytes to gigabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Terabytes to petabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Both are gigabytes to terabytes

questions.explanation: The table compares five properties: main read pattern, main write pattern (random-access low-latency writes from user input versus bulk import via ETL or an event stream), who primarily uses it (end user/customer versus internal analyst for decision support), what the data represents (latest state versus history of events over time), and dataset size.

questions.question: When did analytics move out of OLTP databases, and what was the separate database called?

options.text: In the late 1980s and early 1990s there was a trend for companies to stop using their OLTP systems for analytics purposes and to run the analytics on a separate database instead, called a data warehouse
In the late 1990s, called a data lake
In the 1970s, called a decision support system
In the 2000s, called a lakehouse

questions.explanation: At first the same databases were used for both, since SQL turned out to be quite flexible in this regard.

questions.question: State the two expectations placed on OLTP systems and the harm an ad hoc analytic query does.

options.text: They are usually expected to be highly available and to process transactions with low latency, since they are often critical to the operation of the business. Database administrators therefore closely guard their OLTP databases and are reluctant to let business analysts run ad hoc analytic queries, which are often expensive, scanning large parts of the dataset and harming the performance of concurrently executing transactions
They are expected to be durable and consistent; analytic queries cause data corruption
They are expected to be scalable and cheap; analytic queries exhaust disk space
They are expected to be schema-flexible; analytic queries break the schema

questions.explanation: Resource contention with latency-critical transactions is the specific harm.

questions.question: Define a data warehouse and expand ETL, listing the stages of getting data in.

options.text: A separate database that analysts can query to their hearts' content without affecting OLTP operations, containing a read-only copy of the data in all the various OLTP systems in the company. Data is extracted from OLTP databases using either a periodic data dump or a continuous stream of updates, transformed into an analysis-friendly schema, cleaned up, and then loaded into the data warehouse — a process called Extract-Transform-Load (ETL)
A write-optimized replica of the OLTP database; ETL means Extract-Transfer-Log
A cache of frequently-run reports; ETL means Evaluate-Transform-Load
A distributed file system for raw data; ETL means Export-Translate-Load

questions.explanation: Figure 3-8 shows a simplified outline of ETL into a data warehouse.

questions.question: Why are data warehouses almost unheard of in small companies? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Small companies probably don't have so many different OLTP systems
Most small companies have a small amount of data — small enough that it can be queried in a conventional SQL database, or even analyzed in a spreadsheet
Warehouse software is not available to small companies
Small companies don't run analytics at all

questions.explanation: The chapter closes with the aphorism: in a large company, a lot of heavy lifting is required to do something that is simple in a small company.

questions.question: What is the 'big advantage' of a separate warehouse, and what does the chapter admit about the first half of the chapter?

options.text: The data warehouse can be optimized for analytic access patterns. It turns out that the indexing algorithms discussed in the first half of the chapter work well for OLTP but are not very good at answering analytic queries — so the rest of the chapter looks at storage engines optimized for analytics instead
The advantage is cost; the first half applies equally to analytics
The advantage is durability; the first half was about analytics all along
The advantage is schema flexibility; the first half is superseded

questions.explanation: An unusually direct admission that the preceding forty pages don't transfer.

questions.question: What data model do warehouses commonly use and why, and what looks alike versus different?

options.text: Most commonly relational, because SQL is generally a good fit for analytic queries — there are graphical data analysis tools that generate SQL queries, visualize the results, and allow analysts to explore the data through operations such as drill-down and slicing and dicing. On the surface a warehouse and a relational OLTP database look similar because they both have a SQL query interface, but the internals of the systems can look quite different because they are optimized for very different query patterns. Many database vendors now focus on supporting either transaction processing or analytics workloads, but not both
Most commonly document-oriented, because analytics data is nested
Most commonly graph-oriented, because dimensions are interconnected
Most commonly key-value, because queries are by primary key

questions.explanation: Common interface, divergent internals — which is why a single product rarely excels at both.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about vendors, RedShift, and SQL-on-Hadoop? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Microsoft SQL Server and SAP HANA support transaction processing and analytics in the same product, but are increasingly becoming two separate storage and query engines which happen to be accessible through a common SQL interface
The data warehouse market is dominated by expensive commercial licenses from vendors such as Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA and ParAccel; Amazon RedShift is a hosted version of ParAccel

More recently a plethora of open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects have emerged — Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, Facebook Presto, Apache Tajo and Apache Drill — young but aiming to compete with commercial data warehouse systems, some based on ideas from Google's Dremel
All data warehouses are open source and free of licensing cost

questions.explanation: A snapshot of a market that was splitting along the OLTP/OLAP line.

questions.question: Contrast the variety of data models in transactional and analytic worlds, and give both names for the analytic style.

options.text: Chapter 2 described a wide range of different data models for transaction processing, but in analytics there is much less diversity: many data warehouses are used in a fairly formulaic style known as a star schema, also called dimensional modeling
Analytics has more model diversity; the style is called normalized modeling
Both worlds use only the relational model; the style is called cube modeling
Analytics uses graph models; the style is called network modeling

questions.explanation: Formulaic is the operative word — the shape is highly conventional.

questions.question: What sits at the centre of a star schema, and what does one row mean?

options.text: A fact table — in Figure 3-9's grocery retailer example, fact_sales. Each row represents an event that occurred at a particular time, here a customer's purchase of a product. For website traffic instead, each row would represent a page view or a click by a user
A dimension table; each row represents an entity
A summary table; each row represents an aggregate
A date table; each row represents a day

questions.explanation: Figure 3-9 is an example of a star schema for use in a data warehouse.

questions.question: Why do fact tables get enormous, and what scale does the chapter cite?

options.text: Because facts are captured as individual events rather than pre-aggregated, allowing maximum flexibility of analysis later — at the cost of an extremely large table. A big enterprise like Apple, Walmart or eBay may have tens of petabytes of transaction history in its data warehouse, most of which is in fact tables, running to trillions of rows
Because facts are duplicated per dimension; the cited scale is terabytes
Because facts are never deleted; the cited scale is exabytes at Google
Because facts include all dimension attributes inline; the cited scale is gigabytes

questions.explanation: Dimension tables are usually much smaller — millions of rows — which is why the chapter concentrates primarily on storage of facts.

questions.question: Distinguish the two kinds of columns in a fact table, and give the mnemonic for what dimensions represent.

options.text: Some columns are attributes, such as the price at which the product was sold and the cost of buying it from the supplier (allowing the profit margin to be calculated); other columns are foreign key references to other tables, called dimension tables. As each row in the fact table represents an event, the dimensions represent the who, what, where, when, how, and why of the event
Some columns are keys, others are aggregates; dimensions represent the how much of the event
Some columns are measures, others are timestamps; dimensions represent the order of events
All columns are foreign keys; dimensions represent the schema version

questions.explanation: The who/what/where/when/how/why mnemonic is the chapter's own.

questions.question: What does a dim_product row contain, and why do even dates get a dimension table?

options.text: Each row represents one type of product that is for sale, including its stock-keeping unit (SKU), description, brand name, category, fat content and package size. Even date and time are often represented using dimension tables, because this allows additional information about dates — such as public holidays — to be encoded, allowing queries to differentiate between sales on holidays and non-holidays
Each row represents one sale; dates get a dimension table to save space
Each row represents one supplier; dates get a dimension table for time zones
Each row represents one category; dates are stored inline in the fact table

questions.explanation: Each fact_sales row uses a foreign key to indicate which product was sold in that transaction; for simplicity, if the customer buys several different products at once they are represented as separate rows in the fact table.

questions.question: Explain the name 'star schema', define the snowflake variant, and say which is usually preferred.

options.text: The name comes from the fact that when the table relationships are visualized, the fact table is in the middle surrounded by its dimension tables, like the rays of a star. In the snowflake schema, dimensions are further broken down into subdimensions — for example separate tables for brands and product categories, referenced as foreign keys rather than stored as strings. Snowflake schemas are more normalized than star schemas, but star schemas are often preferred because they are simpler for analysts to work with
The name comes from the star-shaped index; snowflake schemas are always preferred for normalization
The name refers to the fan-out of queries; the two are equivalent
The name comes from the five dimensions; snowflake means denormalized

questions.explanation: Analyst ergonomics beats normalization purity here.

questions.question: How wide are warehouse tables, and what fraction of a fact table row does a typical query actually need?

options.text: Fact tables often have over 100 columns, sometimes several hundred, and dimension tables can also be very wide as they include all the metadata that may be relevant for analysis. A typical data warehouse query only accesses 4 or 5 columns at one time — so roughly 95% or more of each row is loaded and then discarded
Fact tables have about 10 columns and queries use most of them
Fact tables have thousands of columns and queries use half
Fact tables have 100 columns and queries use 80 of them

questions.explanation: SELECT-star queries are rarely needed for analytics. The dim_store table's width is the chapter's evidence for wide dimensions: which services are offered at each store, whether it has an in-store bakery, square footage, the date the store first opened, when it was last remodeled, and how far it is from the nearest highway.

questions.question: Describe row-oriented storage and explain why an index on date_key or product_sk still leaves an analytic query slow.

options.text: In row-oriented storage all the values from one row of a table are stored next to each other (document databases are similar, storing an entire document as one contiguous sequence of bytes). An index tells the storage engine where to find the relevant rows, but it still needs to load all of those rows — each consisting of over 100 attributes — from disk into memory, parse them, and filter out those that don't meet the conditions. That can take a long time
Because the index is not sorted, so a scan is required anyway
Because indexes cannot be used with GROUP BY
Because the index only covers dimension tables

questions.explanation: The index solves row location, not row width — that's the whole motivation for columnar storage.

questions.question: State the column-oriented idea in the chapter's own words.

options.text: Don't store all the values from one row together, but store all the values from each column together instead. If each column is stored in a separate file, a query only needs to read and parse those columns that are used in that query, which can save a lot of work
Store each row twice, once sorted and once unsorted
Store columns in memory and rows on disk
Store only the columns that are indexed

questions.explanation: Figure 3-10 shows storing relational data by column rather than by row.

questions.question: A boxed note guards against a misreading of column storage. What does it say, and what does Parquet demonstrate?

options.text: Column storage is easiest to understand in a relational data model, but it applies equally to nonrelational data — Parquet is a columnar storage format that supports a document data model, based on Google's Dremel. Columnar storage is a physical layout choice, independent of the logical data model
Column storage only works with relational models; Parquet is an exception that proves the rule
Column storage requires a fixed schema; Parquet enforces one
Column storage is a data model, not a layout; Parquet is a data model

questions.explanation: Physical layout versus logical model is the distinction being protected.

questions.question: State the one invariant column-oriented storage relies on.

options.text: Each column file must contain the rows in the same order — so to reassemble an entire row you take the 23rd entry from each of the individual column files and put them together to form the 23rd row of the table
Each column file must be sorted independently by its own values
Each column file must have the same number of bytes
Each column file must contain a copy of the primary key

questions.explanation: Positional correspondence is also what makes bitwise AND across bitmaps valid: the kth bit in one column's bitmap corresponds to the same row as the kth bit in another's.

questions.question: Why does column data compress well, and which technique does the chapter single out for data warehouses?

options.text: The sequences of values for each column often look quite repetitive, which is a good sign for compression; depending on the data, different compression techniques can be used, and one that is particularly effective in data warehouses is bitmap encoding
Column data is always numeric; the technique is delta encoding
Column data is sorted by definition; the technique is dictionary encoding
Column data is small; the technique is gzip

questions.explanation: Figure 3-11 shows compressed, bitmap-indexed storage of a single column. Besides only loading the columns a query requires, compression further reduces the demands on disk throughput.

questions.question: Define bitmap encoding precisely, and explain what is done when the bitmaps are sparse.

options.text: For a column with n distinct values, take n separate bitmaps: one bitmap for each distinct value, with one bit for each row, where the bit is 1 if the row has that value and 0 if not. This works because the number of distinct values in a column is often small compared to the number of rows. If n is bigger there will be a lot of zeros in most of the bitmaps (we say they are sparse), in which case the bitmaps can additionally be run-length encoded, making the encoding of a column remarkably compact
One bitmap per row with one bit per distinct value; sparse bitmaps are discarded
A hash of each value; sparse values are stored as strings
A sorted list of distinct values; sparse columns are not encoded

questions.explanation: For a product_sk column over a billion rows with 100,000 distinct products, raw bitmaps would be 10 to the 14th bits — about 12.5 TB — which is why run-length encoding is essential. The contrasting small-n case: a country column may have approximately 200 distinct values and can be stored with one bit per row.

questions.question: A query filters product_sk to one of three values; another filters product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3. What bitwise operations do these become?
