options.text: The first loads the three bitmaps for those values and computes their bitwise OR, which can be done very efficiently; the second computes the bitwise AND of the two bitmaps. The second is valid because the columns contain the rows in the same order, so the kth bit in one column's bitmap corresponds to the same row as the kth bit in another column's bitmap
The first is an AND, the second an OR; validity comes from sorting
Both are XOR operations; validity comes from checksums
Neither can be done with bitwise operations

questions.explanation: Bitmap indexes such as these are very well suited for the kinds of queries common in a data warehouse.

questions.question: A boxed note calls a common description of Cassandra and HBase 'very misleading'. Which description, and why?

options.text: Calling their column families — a concept inherited from Bigtable — column-oriented. Within each column family they store all columns from a row together, along with a row key, and they do not use column compression; thus the Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented
Calling them row-oriented, when they are truly columnar
Calling them key-value stores, when they are relational
Calling them LSM-based, when they use B-trees

questions.explanation: A widely repeated mislabel the chapter takes care to correct.

questions.question: Disk-to-memory bandwidth is a big bottleneck but not the only one. Which others do developers of analytical databases worry about? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Efficiently using the bandwidth from main memory into the CPU cache
Avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the CPU instruction processing pipeline
Making use of single-instruction-multi-data (SIMD) instructions in modern CPUs
Reducing network round-trips to the storage layer

questions.explanation: The performance story moves from disk down into the CPU.

questions.question: Define vectorized processing and explain how columnar layout helps the CPU.

options.text: A chunk of compressed column data that fits comfortably in the CPU's L1 cache can be iterated through in a tight loop with no function calls, which is much faster than code requiring a lot of function calls and conditions for each record. Column compression allows more rows from a column to fit in the same amount of L1 cache. Operators such as the bitwise AND and OR described previously can be designed to operate on such chunks of compressed column data directly — this technique is known as vectorized processing
Vectorized processing means using GPUs instead of CPUs
Vectorized processing means decompressing data before operating on it, one row at a time
Vectorized processing means parallelizing across machines

questions.explanation: The key point: the operators work on the compressed representation directly, without decompressing first.

questions.question: What order is easiest in a column store, and what does imposing an order buy you?

options.text: It doesn't necessarily matter in which order the rows are stored, so it's easiest to store them in the order in which they were inserted — inserting a new row just means appending to each of the column files. The alternative is to impose an order, as with SSTables, and use that as an indexing mechanism
Sorted order is easiest; imposing insertion order enables compression
Random order is easiest; imposing order enables replication
Reverse insertion order is easiest; imposing order enables deletes

questions.explanation: Sortedness is optional in a column store, and when chosen it doubles as an index.

questions.question: Why can't each column be sorted independently?

options.text: Because then we would no longer know which items in the columns belong to the same row — we can only reconstruct a row because the kth item in one column belongs to the same row as the kth item in another. So the data needs to be sorted an entire row at a time, even though it is stored by column
Because sorting is too expensive per column
Because compression requires a global order
Because the query optimizer expects insertion order

questions.explanation: Positional correspondence is the invariant that independent sorting would destroy.

questions.question: Who picks the sort order in a column store, and what are the first and second sort key examples?

options.text: The administrator of the database, using their knowledge of common queries. If queries often target date ranges such as the last month, making date_key the first sort key lets the query optimizer scan only the rows from the last month, much faster than scanning all rows. A second sort key can determine the order of rows that have the same value in the first column: making product_sk the second sort key groups all sales for the same product on the same day together in storage, helping queries that group or filter sales by product within a certain date range
The query optimizer picks it automatically at query time
The storage engine picks it based on cardinality
The application developer picks it per query

questions.explanation: Sort key choice is a human decision informed by the workload, unlike index selection in an OLTP optimizer.

questions.question: Why does sorting help compression, and how does the effect decay across sort keys?

options.text: If the primary sort column does not have many distinct values, then after sorting it will have long sequences where the same value is repeated many times in a row. A simple run-length encoding could compress that column down to a few kilobytes — even if the table has billions of rows. The effect is strongest on the first sort key; second and third sort keys will be more jumbled up and so won't have such long runs of repeated values, and columns further down the sorting priority appear in essentially random order, so they probably won't compress as well. But having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall
Sorting helps all columns equally, since each is compressed independently
Sorting hurts compression, which is why insertion order is preferred
Sorting only helps numeric columns

questions.explanation: The compression bonus is concentrated in the first sort key and decays fast.

questions.question: Whose idea was storing several different sort orders, and what makes it almost free?

options.text: It was introduced in C-Store and adopted in the commercial data warehouse Vertica. Different queries benefit from different sort orders, so why not store the same data sorted in several different ways? Data needs to be replicated to multiple machines anyway so you don't lose data if one machine fails — you might as well store that redundant data sorted in different ways, so that when processing a query you can use the version that best fits the query pattern
It was introduced in Bigtable and adopted in HBase; it is free because of compression
It was introduced in Dremel and adopted in Parquet; it is free because of columnar layout
It was introduced in Hive; it is free because storage is cheap

questions.explanation: The redundancy you already pay for fault tolerance is repurposed for query performance.

questions.question: Multiple sort orders in a column store are 'a bit similar' to what, and where does the analogy break?

options.text: Similar to having multiple secondary indexes in a row-oriented store. The big difference: the row-oriented store keeps every row in one place (in the heap file or a clustered index) and secondary indexes just contain pointers to the matching rows, whereas in a column store there normally aren't any pointers to data elsewhere, only columns containing values — so each sort order holds the full data
Similar to materialized views; the difference is that views are virtual
Similar to partitioning; the difference is that partitions are disjoint
Similar to replication; the difference is that replicas are identical

questions.explanation: No pointers means each sort order is a complete copy, not a lightweight index.

questions.question: Why do the columnar optimizations make writes difficult? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An update-in-place approach, like B-trees use, is not possible with compressed columns

If you wanted to insert a row in the middle of a sorted table you would most likely have to rewrite all the column files, since rows are identified by their position within a column and the insertion has to update all columns consistently
Column files cannot be appended to at all
Writes require a distributed transaction across column files

questions.explanation: The workload assumption that justifies all of it: most of the load consists of large read-only queries run by analysts. Column-oriented storage, compression and sorting all help make those read queries faster, at the cost of harder writes.

questions.question: What solves the columnar write problem, and who does this?

options.text: LSM-trees, already seen earlier in the chapter. All writes first go to an in-memory store where they are added to a sorted structure and prepared for writing to disk — it doesn't matter whether the in-memory store is row-oriented or column-oriented. When enough writes have accumulated they are merged with the column files on disk and written to new files in bulk. This is essentially what Vertica does
B-trees with a write-ahead log, as used by Parquet
Materialized views, as used by Hive
Anti-caching, as used by C-Store

questions.explanation: The same structure that solved write throughput for OLTP solves it for columnar analytics.

questions.question: With an in-memory write store, what must queries do, and what does the analyst perceive?

options.text: Queries need to examine both the column data on disk and the recent writes in memory, and combine the two — but the query optimizer hides this distinction from the user, so from the analyst's point of view data modified with inserts, updates or deletes is immediately reflected in subsequent queries
Queries read only the disk data, so recent writes are invisible until the next merge
Queries must be re-run after each merge
Queries read only the in-memory store for recent data and require an explicit flag for older data

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes is preserved despite the two-tier storage.

questions.question: Before introducing materialized aggregates, the chapter makes a concession about columnar storage. What does it concede and claim?

options.text: Concedes that not every data warehouse is necessarily a column store — traditional row-oriented databases and a few other architectures are also used; claims that columnar storage can be significantly faster for ad hoc analytical queries, so it is rapidly gaining popularity
Concedes that columnar storage is always slower for ad hoc queries
Concedes that all warehouses are column stores
Claims that row-oriented warehouses are obsolete

questions.explanation: A characteristic move: state the exception before making the general claim.

questions.question: Which SQL aggregate functions does the chapter name, and what is the argument for caching their results?

options.text: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. If the same aggregates are used by many different queries it is wasteful to crunch through the raw data every time — so why not cache some of the counts or sums that queries use most often?
GROUP BY and HAVING; caching is argued against
RANK and DENSE_RANK; caching applies only to window functions
DISTINCT and UNION; caching saves network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Repetition across queries is what makes precomputation pay.

questions.question: Define materialized view versus virtual view, and describe what the SQL engine does when you read from each.

options.text: A standard (virtual) view is a table-like object whose contents are the results of some query; when you read from it, the SQL engine expands it into the view's underlying query on the fly and then processes the expanded query. A materialized view is an actual copy of the query results, written to disk — so a virtual view is just a shortcut for writing queries, while a materialized view stores real data
A materialized view is a shortcut for writing queries; a virtual view is a copy on disk
Both are copies on disk, differing only in refresh policy
Both are expanded on the fly, differing only in caching

questions.explanation: Copy on disk versus expansion at query time is the whole difference.

questions.question: Why must materialized views be maintained, and where do they belong?

options.text: When the underlying data changes a materialized view needs to be updated, because it is a denormalized copy of the data. The database can do that automatically, but such updates make writes more expensive, which is why materialized views are not often used in OLTP databases; in read-heavy data warehouses they can make more sense, though whether they actually improve read performance depends on the individual case
They never need maintenance, since they are recomputed on read
They belong in OLTP databases, where writes are cheap
They must be maintained manually by the analyst

questions.explanation: Note the closing hedge — the chapter declines to promise a read speedup.

questions.question: Give both names for the special case of a materialized view, and describe what aggregating along an axis yields.

options.text: A data cube or OLAP cube: a grid of aggregates grouped by different dimensions. In the two-dimensional case, dates run along one axis and products along the other, and each cell contains the aggregate (e.g. SUM) of an attribute (e.g. net_price) of all facts with that date-product combination. Aggregating along a row or column gives a summary reduced by one dimension — sales by product regardless of date, or sales by date regardless of product
A star cube or fact cube; aggregating along an axis adds a dimension
A snowflake cube or dimension cube; aggregating along an axis yields the raw facts
A hypercube or pivot cube; aggregating along an axis yields a single scalar

questions.explanation: Figure 3-9's schema has five dimensions — date, product, store, promotion and customer — so its full cube is a five-dimensional hypercube, each cell holding the sales for one date-product-store-promotion-customer combination.

questions.question: State the data cube's advantage and its exact disadvantage, plus the policy most warehouses adopt.

options.text: Advantage: certain queries become very fast because they have effectively been precomputed — for total sales per store yesterday you just look at the totals along the appropriate dimension, with no need to scan millions of rows. Disadvantage: a cube doesn't have the same flexibility as querying the raw data — for example there is no way of calculating which proportion of sales comes from items that cost more than $100, because the price isn't one of the dimensions. So most data warehouses try to keep as much raw data as possible and use aggregates such as data cubes only as a performance boost for certain queries
Advantage: cubes save disk space. Disadvantage: they are slow to query. Policy: replace raw data with cubes
Advantage: cubes are always up to date. Disadvantage: they need indexes. Policy: index every dimension
Advantage: cubes support arbitrary queries. Disadvantage: they need maintenance. Policy: discard raw data

questions.explanation: Precomputation buys speed by fixing the questions in advance — which is exactly what it costs you.

questions.question: The Summary splits storage engines in two. Which bottleneck belongs to which?

options.text: OLTP is user-facing with a huge volume of requests that each touch a small number of records by key using an index — disk seek time is often the bottleneck. Analytics systems are used by business analysts rather than end users, handle a much lower volume of queries, but each query is typically very demanding, requiring many millions of records to be scanned in a short time — disk bandwidth, not seek time, is often the bottleneck, and column-oriented storage is an increasingly popular solution
Bandwidth is the OLTP bottleneck; seek time is the analytics bottleneck
Both are bound by seek time
Both are bound by CPU

questions.explanation: Getting the bottlenecks the right way round is the point: seek time for OLTP, bandwidth for OLAP.

questions.question: Name the two OLTP schools of thought and assign the systems the Summary lists.

options.text: The log-structured school, which only permits appending to files and deleting obsolete files but never updates a file that has been written — Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase, Lucene and others. And the update-in-place school, which treats the disk as a set of fixed-size pages that can be overwritten — B-trees being the biggest example, used in all major relational databases and also many nonrelational ones
The row-oriented and column-oriented schools, split between OLTP and OLAP
The in-memory and on-disk schools, split between Redis and PostgreSQL
The hash-index and sorted-index schools, split between Bitcask and B-trees

questions.explanation: Immutability versus overwriting is the deepest division in OLTP storage design.

questions.question: What single idea does the Summary credit log-structured engines with, and why does it matter for hardware?

options.text: They systematically turn random-access writes into sequential writes on disk, which enables higher write throughput due to the performance characteristics of hard drives and SSDs — a comparatively recent development
They eliminate the need for indexes, reducing memory pressure
They compress data, reducing disk capacity requirements
They avoid the write-ahead log, halving write amplification

questions.explanation: Both media are named — the claim is not restricted to spinning disks, though earlier sections say the advantage is most pronounced there.

questions.question: Why does the Summary say analytics stops caring about indexes?

options.text: Because when your queries require sequentially scanning across a large number of rows, indexes are much less relevant; instead it becomes important to encode data very compactly, to minimize the amount of data the query needs to read from disk — and column-oriented storage helps achieve that goal
Because analytic queries always use primary keys
Because indexes cannot be built on fact tables
Because materialized views replace indexes entirely

questions.explanation: The goal shifts from locating rows to minimizing bytes read.

questions.question: What does the chapter claim for you at the end, and what does it disclaim?

options.text: Claims that armed with this knowledge of storage engine internals you are in a much better position to know which tool is best suited for your application, and that when you need to adjust a database's tuning parameters this understanding lets you imagine what effect a higher or lower value may have. Disclaims that although the chapter couldn't make you an expert in tuning any one particular storage engine, it has hopefully given you enough vocabulary and ideas to make sense of the documentation for the database of your choice
Claims you can now implement your own storage engine; disclaims nothing
Claims you can now tune any engine expertly; disclaims the OLAP material
Claims nothing; disclaims the whole chapter as background

questions.explanation: Which matches the promise made at the start: you need a rough idea of what the storage engine is doing under the hood, not expertise.
